item.title: llama-server Context Overflow: Reading the "exceeds the available context size" Error and Finding Which Part of Your Agent's Prompt Caused It (2026)
item.description: Four different llama.cpp server mechanisms produce a dead or damaged agent turn at the context line. Here is how to tell them apart from the error payload, the finish_reason and the server log, and how to attribute the overflow to a named section of your prompt.
item.content:encoded:
An agent that has been working against a self-hosted llama.cpp server for twenty or forty turns eventually stops working, and the symptom is almost never specific enough to act on: a half-written answer, an empty completion, a tool call that never arrives, or a request that never gets a reply at all. The tempting response is to raise -c, which is exactly the fix that KV memory may not allow, and which does nothing for the two of the four failure modes below that are not really about running out of room.

This article maps four distinct mechanisms in the server, each with the source location that produces it, and then gives a procedure for attributing the overflow to a named section of the request. Everything here is read from tools/server at a pinned commit plus upstream reports; the companion question of which advertised window a model actually supports is covered separately in the context-window comparison, and where llama-server sits among other local servers is covered in the serving-framework survey.

The code citations below are against commit 369dcf309c8b274370e692ac2d42d9708597ae04 (2026-10-29). server-context.cpp at that commit is byte-identical to the same file at the v0.8.0 release tag target 8642541b255bfb5dc39cd351a178be09013a55d6 (sha256 26acff2657377779f0b48317c043c97b6e9022eaf89d8d956d8ae2a8b2e6e38d, 304170 bytes), so the shift logic described in Outcome 3 is shipped behaviour rather than unreleased master. Byte equality of one file is not proof that a released binary behaves identically, but it does rule out the possibility that the tag predates this code.

The four ways a turn dies at the context line

Outcome What the client sees Where it comes from What tells it apart
Arrival rejection an error before any token; n_prompt_tokens and n_ctx in the body request-size check on admission the error message itself
Clean limit stop text ending mid-sentence, finish_reason: "length" generation-side capacity check finish_reason alone cannot distinguish it from a max_tokens cut
Middle-slice shift no error; generation continues over a prompt with a slice removed --context-shift compaction the slot context shift warning’s n_keep, which fixes where the hole is
Checkpoint re-prefill slow but correct; nothing overflows checkpoint invalidation on hybrid, recurrent and SWA models prompt_n on every turn

Match your symptom to a row before you change a flag. Two of the four rows are silent, which is why “the model got dumber after twenty turns” and “the server rejected my request” are sometimes the same problem and sometimes not.

Outcome 1: the request is rejected before a single token

On the chat path the server compares the tokenised request against the slot’s context size on admission and refuses anything at or above the limit, in server-context.cpp around line 4081:

if (slot.task->n_tokens() >= slot.n_ctx) {
    send_error(slot, string_format("request (%d tokens) exceeds the available context size (%d tokens), try increasing it", ...),
               ERROR_TYPE_EXCEED_CONTEXT_SIZE);
    slot.release();

Three details matter when you are reading your own logs. The comparison is >=, not >, so a prompt exactly equal to n_ctx is rejected. The slot is released before decoding, so nothing was generated and no partial answer exists to inspect. And this branch only applies to prompts the scheduler is allowed to split: a task that must be processed in one batch — an embedding-style request, a reranker whose pooling is not LAST, a decision over a non-causal context — takes the parallel branch above it, which uses a strict > test and different wording, “input (N tokens) is larger than the max context size (M tokens). skipping”. That is why grepping for the chat message turns up nothing on an embeddings endpoint, and why the two messages are not interchangeable.

The rejection is at least self-diagnosing, because the error object carries the two numbers that define the gap. In server-task.cpp the error serializer adds them only for this error type:

if (err_type == ERROR_TYPE_EXCEED_CONTEXT_SIZE) {
    res["n_prompt_tokens"] = n_prompt_tokens;
    res["n_ctx"]           = n_ctx;
}

So the useful log line from a client is not “context exceeded” but the pair of numbers: if n_prompt_tokens is 1.2× n_ctx you have a prompt-building bug (a re-injected reasoning block, a tool schema repeated per turn, a transcript that grows without bound), and if it is 1.01× you have a near-miss that a small history cap will fix. Upstream has both shapes: a report of a prompt at roughly three times the configured window being accepted and then hard-failing (#28848, closed as not planned on 2026-10-29), and reports of long interactions simply stopping (#19636, closed as duplicate). The request to truncate history server-side instead of returning an error was filed in November 2025 and closed without the behaviour changing (#17284).

Outcome 2: generation stops and the stream says “length”

If the prompt fits at admission but the answer would push past the window, the interesting thing happens during generation. With context shift at its default — disabled — process_token checks capacity after each token and, on running out, marks the slot rather than raising an error:

if (!params_base.ctx_shift && slot.prompt.n_tokens() + 1 >= slot.n_ctx) {
    slot.truncated      = true;
    slot.stop           = STOP_TYPE_LIMIT;
    slot.has_next_token = false;

There is also a later guard in pre_decode that sends send_error(slot, "context shift is disabled", ...) if generation somehow reaches the boundary, and the source labels it as redundant: “we should never get here, because generation should already stopped in process_token()”. So the common case is a clean stop rather than a broken connection, and the only trace it leaves in the stream is the finish reason discussed next.

The clean stop is where the diagnosis gets hard, because the OpenAI-compatible chat stream collapses the cause. In to_json_oaicompat_chat_stream() the finish reason starts at "length" and is only replaced when the stop was a stop-word or end-of-sequence:

std::string finish_reason = "length";
if (stop == STOP_TYPE_WORD || stop == STOP_TYPE_EOS) {
    finish_reason = oaicompat_msg.tool_calls.empty() ? "stop" : "tool_calls";
}

Everything that is not a word or an EOS — including the capacity limit above — reports "length". The two fields that would name the cause, truncated and stop_type, exist only in the native /completion serializer to_json_non_oaicompat(), which is not what an OpenAI-compatible chat client receives. The practical consequence is blunt: on the /v1/chat/completions path, finish_reason: "length" cannot tell you whether the server ran out of context or your client’s max_tokens was simply too small. The discriminator has to come from elsewhere — a n_prompt_tokens versus n_ctx comparison on the next request, the server stdout, or the native endpoint during a debugging session.

Outcome 3: –context-shift deletes a hole, not the tail

Enabling context shift does not make the server truncate the oldest turns, nor the newest: it deletes one contiguous slice at a position set by n_keep, then continues. The whole block is worth reading because the default is the variant that lands at the front of your prompt:

int n_keep = slot.task->params.n_keep < 0 ? slot.task->n_tokens() : slot.task->params.n_keep;

if (add_bos_token) {
    n_keep += 1;
}

n_keep = std::min(slot.n_ctx - 4, n_keep);
const int n_left    = slot.prompt.n_tokens() - n_keep;
int       n_discard = slot.task->params.n_discard ? slot.task->params.n_discard : (n_left / 2);
n_discard = std::clamp(n_discard, 0, std::max(0, n_left - 1));
SLT_WRN(slot, "slot context shift, n_keep = %d, n_left = %d, n_discard = %d\n", n_keep, n_left, n_discard);
slot.mem.seq_rm (slot.id, n_keep            , n_keep + n_discard);
slot.mem.seq_add(slot.id, n_keep + n_discard, slot.prompt.tokens.pos_next(), -n_discard);

Read the default literally, because it decides where the hole lands, and the answer is the one nobody expects. The field n_keep defaults to 0 — the README says “By default, this value is set to 0, meaning no tokens are kept. Use -1 to retain all tokens from the prompt”, and common.h initialises n_keep = 0 on the params struct — so a request that omits the field arrives with zero. The ternary takes the else arm and keeps 0, or 1 when the chat template sets add_bos_token and the BOS token is added immediately after the branch. n_left is then the whole prompt, n_discard defaults to half of it, and seq_rm removes [0 or 1, n_discard): the head of the request goes first. In an agent request that means the system message and the tool schemas at position zero, then the oldest turns in order. On a prompt that is mostly history, your agent loses its instructions before it loses its oldest tool output, and what continues to be generated is an answer the model is no longer being told how to format.

The other two settings move the boundary, and they are the ones people assume are the default. n_keep = -1 is the explicit keep-all variant: the ternary substitutes slot.task->n_tokens(), the entire incoming request, so n_left is only what has been generated since admission and the removed range [n_keep, n_keep + n_discard) starts exactly at the end of the request. The first half of the answer already streaming to your client is deleted while the conversation in the request survives intact; nothing in the request is touched, but the text you already showed the user no longer corresponds to the state the model continues from.

An explicit positive keep count is the third case, and the only one that gives a middle-of-history slice. With n_keep set to a value smaller than the prompt — the --keep N flag or the request field — everything up to n_keep survives, the next n_discard tokens of history are removed, and the tail of the conversation is kept. That is the configuration where an agent loses the middle of its transcript and keeps answering plausibly, with the system prompt and tool schemas still in place.

Nothing in the stream announces any of the three. The only artefact is the slot context shift, n_keep = ..., n_left = ..., n_discard = ... warning on the server’s stderr, and the three numbers tell you which variant you got: an n_keep of 0 or 1 means the deleted range began at the head of the prompt, an n_keep close to the size of the request means it began inside the generated text, and a value between the two means it began in the history.

Two configurations refuse to shift at all rather than shift badly. A task with more than one completion — n_cmpl > 1 — becomes a parent task plus child slots launched by launch_slots_with_parent_task() (server-context.cpp lines 2674-2710 in the same file), which share one prompt; the guard if (slot.task->is_parent() || slot.task->is_child()) at lines 3784-3786 rejects either of them with send_error(slot, "context shift cannot be used for shared prompt", ...). A multimodal context aborts with not supported by multimodal if the auto-disable path is ever bypassed. Context shift is not a safety net for shared-prompt multi-completion requests, nor for vision models.

Outcome 4: nothing overflows and it is still slow

The fourth mechanism does not involve overflow at all, and mistaking it for one is expensive because the fix is the opposite of raising -c. On hybrid and recurrent architectures the context checkpoints that make incremental prefill possible are invalidated, and on /slots restore they are not persisted, so the server reprocesses the whole prompt every turn while the numbers stay comfortably inside the window. Three upstream reports cover the parts: checkpoints always invalidated on hybrid/recurrent models (#24055), no KV reuse from /slots restore on hybrid/recurrent and sliding-window models because checkpoints are not serialised (#28194), and no checkpoint created at the end of the system prompt, so a client that renders its own prompts re-prefills where a client that lets the server render does not — the reporter compares prompt_n of 1214 against 9 for the same content (#30783). All three are issue reports, not measurements reproduced here.

The discriminator is prompt_n in the response timings, or the per-turn timing block in the server log. Stable prompt_n near the size of the newly added content means reuse is working. prompt_n growing with the length of the whole conversation means every turn is a cold prefill, and the answer is a prompt-cache or architecture problem, not a context-size problem.

Attributing the window to a named section of your prompt

Once you know which outcome you hit, the next question is which part of the request consumed the window, because “raise -c” is not available when the KV cache is what is binding. A cheap way to answer it is to tokenise the request yourself, per section, and compare against the server’s own n_ctx from GET /props.

Capture one real request body from your client — the exact JSON that the agent sends, tools array included — and run it through the tokenizer for the same model:

curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/props | jq '{n_ctx: .default_generation_settings.n_ctx}'
curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/tokenize -d @request.json | jq '.tokens | length'

Then split the body and repeat: the tools array alone, the messages array, and the messages[*].content of each assistant turn that carries a reasoning echo. The expected ranking is tool JSON schemas and accumulated history ahead of the system prompt, but the ratios differ enough between frameworks that guessing is unreliable, and the only way to see the section you did not think of is to count it.

Two rules make the count trustworthy. Use the tokenizer the server uses, not an approximation from a different model family, or the per-section split will be right in relative terms and wrong in the absolute terms you need against n_ctx. And keep the request you measured: if you later trim a section and the total does not drop by roughly the amount you removed, your client is rebuilding the payload, and the number you measured is not the number the server received.

For per-turn accounting across a whole run rather than one request, the trajectory-monitor approach in agent trajectory monitoring for tool calls and token spend records the same numbers over time, which is what distinguishes a prompt that grows linearly from one that grows per tool call.

What to change before you raise -c

Order the fixes by cost, not by comfort. The cheapest change is the one that does not touch the server at all.

Cap history at a section boundary your agent understands — a completed tool call, not an arbitrary token offset — so the truncation you perform is one you can reason about. Prune the tool schemas the current turn cannot use; a large tool surface is resent on every request and is invisible in a transcript. Treat --context-shift as a setting that needs a deliberate --keep: with the request default n_keep of 0 the shift deletes the leading slice, system message and tool schemas first, while --keep -1 protects the whole request and puts the hole inside the answer you are streaming, and only an explicit positive keep-region that covers the system prompt and the tool schemas makes the deletion land on older turns instead. Only then look at -c: the README documents -c as defaulting to 0 (take the model’s own training context), --context-shift as disabled by default, and --kv-unified-per-slot N as sizing the shared pool to n_parallel * N when -c is unset, which is the flag that makes per-slot limits predictable when you run several agents against one process. Context checkpoints default to 32 with a minimum spacing of 8192 tokens, so on a model with a long prompt and no checkpoint at the system-prompt boundary, raising -c buys memory pressure without buying reuse.

The client-side half of this — what to keep in a working set, when to compact — is covered in context engineering for coding agents and in the token-waste reduction guide. This article is deliberately only about what the server does when you cross the line, which is a different question from what you should have sent.

What the server does and does not tell you

The contract, as read at the pinned commit:

  • Arrival rejection is explicit and carries n_prompt_tokens and n_ctx.
  • A generation-time capacity stop on the OpenAI-compatible chat stream is reported as finish_reason: "length", indistinguishable from a max_tokens cut.
  • The native /completion response adds truncated and stop_type, which is why a one-off reproduction against /completion is worth the trouble when the chat path is ambiguous.
  • --context-shift reports itself only as a slot context shift, n_keep = ..., n_left = ..., n_discard = ... warning on stderr, and the values are the only way to know whether the discard landed in the request or in the generated text.
  • Checkpoint behaviour is not surfaced at all except through prompt_n and the timing block.

The closing caveat is the one that costs people days: a clean stream is not proof of an intact prompt. Outcome 2 and Outcome 3 both produce plausible text, and only the log distinguishes “the model gave a short answer” from “the server deleted a slice of the prompt, or of the answer, and kept going”.

Upstream may change any of this; the behaviour described here is pinned to the commit named above, and between 369dcf30 and the later master 36a0e2ffc0b352b774f8d71c43668b75b3061ef5 the shift block and the admission test were unchanged, so no safe tail truncation landed in that window either.

Primary sources

  • tools/server/server-context.cpp at 369dcf30 — https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/369dcf309c8b274370e692ac2d42d9708597ae04/tools/server/server-context.cpp
  • tools/server/server-task.cpp at 369dcf30 — https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/369dcf309c8b274370e692ac2d42d9708597ae04/tools/server/server-task.cpp
  • server README (flag defaults) at 369dcf30 — https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/369dcf309c8b274370e692ac2d42d9708597ae04/tools/server/README.md
  • common/common.h (the n_keep = 0 default on common_params) at 369dcf30 — https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/369dcf309c8b274370e692ac2d42d9708597ae04/common/common.h
  • same file at later master 36a0e2ff — https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/36a0e2ffc0b352b774f8d71c43668b75b3061ef5/tools/server/server-context.cpp
  • same file at v0.8.0 tag target 8642541b — https://raw.githubusercontent.com/ggml-org/llama.cpp/8642541b255bfb5dc39cd351a178be09013a55d6/tools/server/server-context.cpp
  • upstream reports, states as fetched on 2026-10-30: #17284 (closed), #19636 (closed), #25566 (closed), #28848 (closed as not planned), #30783 (open), #24055 (open), #28194 (open).

Incidence, as a reader-pain proxy only: a GitHub issue search for the exact error string returned 17 issues spanning 2025-02-23 to 2026-09-30, and a title search for “context size” among issues created after 2026-07-01 returned 10. Both are text-match counts read on 2026-10-30 at 06:12 UTC; they include issues that merely quote the string, and no search volume or traffic estimate is claimed.

Verification note

Every quoted excerpt above was checked against the saved raw response for the URL it is attributed to, at the fetched bytes, and the issue states were read from the GitHub API responses on 2026-10-30 between 06:11 and 06:13 UTC. No llama.cpp build was executed for this article: there is no server binary or GGUF weights in the authoring environment, so no token counts, timings, finish_reason values or shift log lines are presented as observed. The procedures in the attribution section are commands for you to run against your own server; they are not a dataset shipped with this page.

item.title: MCP stdio Leaks: Why Your Agent's Tool Servers Hang at Shutdown, Die on a Bad Filename and Leave Ghost Tools
item.description: Four stdio lifecycle failures in the MCP Python SDK 2.2.0, measured with a probe that counts processes and tools — plus a shutdown contract your agent host can enforce.
item.content:encoded:
A stdio MCP server that never exits is not a mystery: the Python SDK’s writer task can be blocked in a pipe write that only the reader can unblock, so cancelling it waits forever. In MCP Python SDK 2.2.0 on Linux, this probe reproduced that hang and three related lifecycle defects — an unencodable string that kills the connection with no JSON-RPC error, a rejected ClientSessionGroup registration that leaves a second server child alive and unreachable, and a disconnected session whose old tool name survives in group.tools. All four have a host-side workaround you can enforce today, and the probe below counts exactly what your host leaks.

The article is about what happens after the handshake. If you are still writing your first server, start with building an MCP server in Python or the FastMCP 3 guide and come back here when your process table starts to fill.

The four symptoms, one accounting frame

Symptom in production Where it comes from What the probe recorded on mcp 2.2.0
Server never exits after the session ends stdout write blocked on a full pipe; cancellation waits on the thread alive 10 s after stdin EOF, SIGTERM needed, exit status −15
One session dies, no error in the client serialisation inside the writer task is not contained PydanticSerializationError, 0 bytes written, connection gone
Extra server process after a failed connect transport opened before components are validated 2 children, 1 session in the group, 0 children only after group close
Tool the model calls no longer exists reverse index replaced, aggregate dict updated only old still in group.tools after disconnect, group.sessions == []

L1: the hang is a full pipe, not a missing exit

The mechanism is a Linux pipe: 64 KiB of buffered bytes, then write(2) blocks. The SDK’s server writer serialises each outgoing message and writes it with stdout.write plus stdout.flush inside a worker thread (to_thread). If the client stops draining stdout while a response larger than the buffer is still in flight, that thread is stuck in the kernel. When stdin EOF then ends the session, the task group cancels the writer — and cancellation has to wait for a thread that cannot finish until the client reads.

The probe drives the same sequence twice: one response of 262,144 payload bytes, stdin closed 2 s later, 10 s of /proc sampling, then SIGTERM.

Arm stdout bytes read State 10 s after EOF Signal needed Exit status
Drain stdout (control) 262,190 exited none 0
Leave stdout unread 0 S (sleeping) SIGTERM −15

The control arm is what makes this a finding rather than a fixture bug: identical fixture, identical message, only the read side differs. With the reader draining, the process exits 0 by itself. Without a reader, it is still alive after ten seconds and has to be signalled. This is the same sequence reported upstream in issue #3674, where the reporter’s thread dump shows a worker blocked behind await stdout.flush() in mcp/server/stdio.py.

Host-side consequence: closing stdin is not a shutdown. Any supervisor that only closes the pipe and waits will accumulate one sleeping child per session.

L2: one unencodable string takes the whole connection

A str containing a lone surrogate cannot be encoded as UTF-8 JSON. It is easy to obtain without any malicious input: os.fsdecode() on a filename that is not valid UTF-8 returns one, and so does open(..., errors="surrogateescape") or a decoded argv. Validation passes, model_dump(mode="json") passes, and the failure lands in model_dump_json() inside the writer task, where only anyio.ClosedResourceError is caught.

In the probe the server sent one response whose uri field was built from os.fsdecode(b"bad-\xff-name"), then tried to send a second, valid message:

  • stdout bytes delivered to the client: 0 — not even the bad message, because serialisation fails before the write.
  • stderr: pydantic_core._pydantic_core.PydanticSerializationError: Error serializing to JSON: UnicodeEncodeError: 'utf-8' codec can't encode character '\udcff' in position 4: surrogates not allowed.
  • The writer task ended, the task group tore down the session, and the fixture exited with an ExceptionGroup — the caller learns nothing about which request failed.

That matches issue #3707, where the reporter describes the same class of failure for the server writer and for the client’s stdin_writer on every transport. The exception class depends on the resolved pydantic version; this run used pydantic 2.14.2, so treat PydanticSerializationError as the shape, not the contract.

Host-side consequence: a single path, filename, or environment value that survives surrogateescape can kill a session, and the failure surfaces as a closed connection rather than an error for that request. Sanitise outbound payloads at the boundary (json.dumps(..., ensure_ascii=True) or explicit re-encoding with errors=“replace”) if any of your tool inputs come from the filesystem.

L3: who owns a transport whose connect was rejected

ClientSessionGroup.connect_to_server starts the transport, initialises the session, and only then aggregates components. The duplicate-name check raises before the session is recorded:

matching_tools = tools_temp.keys() & self._tools.keys()
if matching_tools:
    raise MCPError(code=types.INVALID_PARAMS, message=f"{matching_tools} already exist in group tools.")

# Aggregate components.
self._sessions[session] = component_names

That ordering is visible in the v2.2.0 source of session_group.py, and the probe confirms the runtime effect: after the rejected second connect, len(group.sessions) is still 1 while the process table shows 2 children. The caller has no session object, so disconnect_from_server() cannot reach the transport; only closing the whole group reclaimed it (0 children after close).

This is issue #3490. The caveat matters for your fix: it is a lifetime-scope mismatch, not an unbounded orphan. The second child lives until the group closes. In a long-lived host that keeps one group open for hours and re-registers servers per reconnect, that is still one leaked process per rejection.

L4: ghost tools survive disconnect

The same aggregation path keeps an older catalogue. The probe registered one caller-owned session whose server advertised old, changed the server’s catalogue to new, registered the same session again, then disconnected:

Step group.tools group.sessions
First registration ['old'] 1
Second registration ['new', 'old'] 1
After disconnect_from_server ['old'] 0

Disconnect removes only the names in the current reverse index for that session, while the aggregate dictionaries were merged on both registrations. That is issue #3713, reported with exactly this shape. The model keeps a tool in its prompt that the host can no longer route.

A shutdown contract your host can enforce

None of these need a fork of the SDK. They need four rules in the code that owns the child process:

  1. Close stdin, then drain stdout, then wait. Never expect EOF alone to end a server whose response is still in a pipe. Read until EOF before you join the process, and put a wall-clock bound on the join.
  2. Escalate on a bound, and record which signal worked. A server that ignores EOF is normal in this class; a server that survives SIGTERM is a different bug. Log both transitions with the pid so the next leak is countable.
  3. Close the transport on a failed connect, not just on a returned session. Wrap connect_to_server yourself: on exception, close the group (or the transport you opened) before retrying, because the handle you would need was never returned.
  4. Verify the tool table after every disconnect. assert not group.tools (or compare against the set you expect) is a one-line test that catches the ghost-tool class before a model tries to call a tool that is gone.

If you want the accounting view alongside this, the OpenTelemetry trace setup in agent observability with OpenTelemetry shows the span side, and agent doctor covers local runtime health checks that can host the process-count assertion above.

The probe: what it counts and what it does not

probe_stdio_lifecycle.py spawns real stdio children against mcp==2.2.0, samples /proc/<pid>/stat for state, walks /proc for children of the test process, and records stdout byte counts plus stderr text per scenario. It is not a harness for your own servers; it is a small reproducible check of the SDK paths above.

Files from this run, published with the article (origin: first-party run on 2026-10-30, Linux, CPython 3.12.3, no personal data):

  • probe_stdio_lifecycle.py
  • fixture_server.py
  • fixture_stdio_writer.py
  • results.json (raw records)
  • method.md

Limits, stated plainly: one Linux host, one run per arm, one pinned version (2.2.0), fixture servers written for this article rather than third-party servers. L3 and L4 were executed in a second invocation of the same probe (--only L3,L4) and merged into results.json; timestamps in the record show both windows. The 64 KiB pipe buffer is a Linux default — macOS and Windows pipe sizes differ, and none of the timing or signal behaviour here should be transferred to them without re-running. v2.3.0 ships different bytes for session_group.py and client/stdio.py, so “still broken in 2.3.0” is not established by this run; the server writer path was byte-identical between the two tags when the sources were fetched.

If you do not run the probe, the four rules above still hold: they are derived from the source paths quoted here, not from a benchmark score.

Sources

  • modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk#3674 — stdio server never exits on stdin EOF while the client leaves stdout unread.
  • modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk#3707 — a lone surrogate in an outgoing message kills the writer or the session.
  • modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk#3490 — a rejected connect_to_server leaves its transport running.
  • modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk#3713 — old tools survive after disconnecting a re-registered session.
  • modelcontextprotocol/python-sdk#3714 — strict decoding withholds fatal read errors until peer stdout EOF.
  • mcp/server/stdio.py at v2.2.0 — the writer task and its single except clause.
  • mcp/client/stdio.py at v2.2.0 — the shielded _drain_stdout in finally, and the process-stop escalation order.
  • mcp/client/session_group.py at v2.2.0 — the raise-before-record ordering and the disconnect loop over the current index.

item.title: When an Expired Memory Blocks the New One: mem0 OSS Expiry, Deduplication and the Write That Never Lands
item.description: On mem0ai 2.2.1 an expired memory still reaches the extraction prompt and the md5 dedup set, so a fresh add() of the same fact returns an empty list. Read the code path, the provider call an expiry update still makes, and a delete-then-add workaround.
item.content:encoded:
Your agent stored user prefers aisle seats with an expiration date. The date passed. The user says it again. You call add() with a fresh expiration_date, get no exception, get an empty results list, and get_all() shows nothing. The fact never lands, and it will never land as long as the expired copy is what the search returns.

On mem0ai 2.2.1 — the Python OSS package, self-hosted — the cause is a read/write asymmetry. Expiration is applied as a filter on the read paths but not on the ADD path. The expired row is still handed to the extraction LLM as an “existing memory”, and its hash is still loaded into the dedup set, so the fresh write is dropped as a duplicate of a record the user can no longer see. The same write machinery adds a second dependency: an update that only touches metadata or the expiry date still calls the embedding provider, and a provider error stops that update before anything is persisted.

This article walks the exact code path at a pinned tag, separates what is verified in source from what is only reported in the issue tracker, and gives a write pattern that does not depend on a fix shipping.

Everything below is scoped to mem0ai==2.2.1 (Python, self-hosted vector store). The hosted platform is out of scope, and no recall or accuracy benchmark is claimed.

The two-minute check

Before reading further, decide which failure you actually have. The first two look identical from the caller’s side — a successful call, no error, nothing visible. The third surfaces as an update that failed or changed nothing.

mem = Memory.from_config(cfg)          # pinned: mem0ai==2.2.1
res = mem.add("user prefers aisle seats", user_id=u,
              expiration_date="2026-11-30")   # future date, same fact as an expired row
print(res)                                  # empty results means the write was suppressed
# get_all() takes entity scope inside `filters`; top-level user_id is rejected on 2.2.1
print(mem.get_all(filters={"user_id": u})["results"])                     # expired rows stay hidden
print(mem.get_all(filters={"user_id": u}, show_expired=True)["results"])  # the ghost row is still there

If results is empty while show_expired=True still lists the old row, you are in the expired-record suppression case. If the date itself is impossible (2099-02-30), you are in the CLI validation case. If a metadata-only or expiry-only update() raises a provider error — or leaves the record unchanged because your retry wrapper swallowed one — you are in the unnecessary-embedding path described in issue #7561, covered below.

Expiration in 2.2.1 hides a record; it does not delete it

_payload_is_expired compares the stored expiration_date against today’s UTC date, and both get_all() and search() skip rows it flags unless show_expired=True is passed. The helper spans lines 442-451 of mem0/memory/main.py at tag v2.2.1, with the comparison at line 449 and the except ValueError: return False closing it at 450-451. The read-path filters are applied at lines 1369 and 1684. Because the date comparison is < now, a memory that expires today is still visible today.

That is a visibility filter over live rows, not a deletion and not a tombstone. Nothing in the expiry helper removes the vector, and there is no expiry-driven cleanup pass in the file. So the row keeps its payload, keeps its hash, and keeps being a candidate for any code path that does not call _payload_is_expired. Source: mem0ai/mem0 v2.2.1 main.py.

The ADD path never applies that filter

_add_to_vector_store() runs in phases. Phase 1 retrieves candidate existing memories with vector_store.search(...) at top_k=10 and immediately maps them into the extraction prompt without checking expiry (lines 925-943):

# Phase 1: Existing memory retrieval
existing_results = self.vector_store.search(
    query=parsed_messages,
    vectors=query_embedding,
    top_k=10,
    filters=search_filters,
)
...
existing_memories.append({"id": str(idx), "text": mem.payload.get("data", "")})

Phase 5 then builds the dedup set from the same unfiltered list (lines 1007-1013):

# Phase 4: Per-memory CPU processing + Phase 5: Hash dedup
existing_hashes = set()
for mem in existing_results:
    h = mem.payload.get("hash") if hasattr(mem, "payload") and mem.payload else None
    if h:
        existing_hashes.add(h)

Two consequences follow, and only one of them is obvious.

The first is prompt contamination. The extraction LLM receives the expired text inside the “existing memories” block. With an additive prompt, the model is being asked whether the incoming statement adds anything new relative to what it is shown — and it is shown the expired copy. So the model can legitimately decide there is nothing new to extract, and return no memories at all.

The second is silent deduplication. If extraction does emit the text, the loop at lines 1022-1025 computes hashlib.md5(text.encode()).hexdigest() and skips the record when that hash is in existing_hashes. The expired row’s hash is in that set.

Both routes end at the same branch. When every candidate record is skipped, the function saves the messages for context and returns an empty list to add() (lines 1043-1045, with return [] at line 1045). No exception, no warning at default log level — the caller sees a successful-shaped result object with nothing in it.

This is the mechanism the reporter describes in mem0ai/mem0#7612, which reports it for both Memory and AsyncMemory. The issue is open, created 2026-10-12, with three comments at the time this analysis read it.

Why the suppression is deterministic only sometimes

The dedup gate is md5 over the exact extracted string, not over a normalized form and not over a semantic embedding. text_lemmatized is computed for BM25, and it is stored in the payload, but it is not what participates in deduplication.

That has a practical implication for anyone trying to reproduce the bug: the failure is exact only when the extraction LLM emits the same characters as the stored, expired copy. Rephrase the fact (aisle seats versus prefers an aisle seat) and the hash differs, the dedup check passes, and a new row is written — while the stale one stays hidden. Two readers with the same package version can therefore disagree about whether the bug exists, depending on their prompt and model. Treat “reproduces” as “same extraction text on the same top-10 result set”, not as a version-level guarantee.

The contaminated-prompt half of the mechanism is softer still, because it depends on how the model reacts to seeing its own expired text. Source-level inspection establishes that the expired row is passed in; it cannot establish what a given model does with it.

The other half: clearing an expiry still calls the embedding provider

If the row is hidden rather than deleted, the obvious repair is to clear its expiry and let the next add() update it in place. In the Python SDK at 2.2.1 the field handling works: update() takes expiration_date with a sentinel default, and an explicit None normalizes to None, which _payload_is_expired treats as “no expiry”:

if expiration_date is not _UNSET:
    update_metadata = update_metadata or {}
    update_metadata["expiration_date"] = _normalize_expiration_date(expiration_date)

That is lines 1871-1873, and _normalize_expiration_date(None) returns None at lines 427-429. Note the sentinel: omitting the argument leaves the field alone, while passing None clears it. Collapsing those two cases in your own wrapper is how you get an “update that silently removes the expiry”.

What the SDK does not give you is a free clear. update() itself embeds only when you pass new text — lines 1875-1877 leave the map empty otherwise:

existing_embeddings = {}
if text is not None:
    existing_embeddings[text] = self.embedding_model.embed(text, "update")

That guard is where a source skim stops, and it is not the last word on the call path. update() passes the map to _update_memory() at line 1879. There, a missing data argument is replaced with the stored text (lines 2065-2067), and the embedding step is a cache-or-embed:

if data in existing_embeddings:
    embeddings = existing_embeddings[data]
else:
    embeddings = self.embedding_model.embed(data, "update")

For a metadata-only or expiry-only call the map is empty, so the else branch always runs: line 2085 embeds the unchanged text, and only then does line 2087 write the payload through vector_store.update. The provider call is unnecessary — the vector cannot change — but it sits on the critical path. If it raises, the payload write is never reached, and the expiry is still set on the stored row.

That is exactly what mem0ai/mem0#7561 reports: each metadata-only, expiration-set and expiration-clear operation calls embedding once, and injecting an embedding APIConnectionError prevents the update while the existing record stays intact. The issue is open, created 2026-10-07, with four comments when read on 2026-10-28, and its environment block names an installed mem0ai 2.2.1 distribution running against a real Memory/AsyncMemory, a temporary local Qdrant and in-memory SQLite, mocking only the external OpenAI Embeddings.create boundary. That is the same code the excerpts above come from, which is why this is a confirmed defect on the pinned version rather than an ageing report.

So the clear is conditional: it works when your embedding provider is healthy — at the cost of one embedding call the operation does not need — and raises before persisting when it is not. If the provider is the component that is failing, treat delete-then-add as the fallback rather than the clear, with the caveat in the workaround section that add() embeds too: the fallback changes which failure you see, not whether a provider is needed.

The CLIs are worse off. Both expose --expires to set an expiration and neither exposes a clear operation, and their platform backends only attach expiration_date when the value is truthy, so an explicit null is dropped rather than sent as a clear. That gap is documented in mem0ai/mem0#7699, open since 2026-10-21. If your agent’s memory maintenance runs through the CLI, the SDK escape hatch is not reachable from it — you need the SDK path or an explicit delete.

The third path: an impossible date that escapes validation

2099-02-30 is correctly shaped and impossible. Per mem0ai/mem0#7713 (open, created 2026-10-23), the Python CLI’s shared _validate_expires() helper lets such a date reach date.fromisoformat, which raises ValueError — uncaught, and in agent mode outside the normal JSON error envelope, so a calling agent gets a traceback-shaped failure instead of a structured error it can branch on.

The reporter’s reproduction invokes the real Typer parser with a mocked backend and telemetry disabled; no credentials or live HTTP requests are involved. That is a valid way to test input validation, and it is also why the article treats this as a reported CLI defect rather than something verified against a live install here: the CLI ships separately from the mem0ai wheel, so a wheel-version pin does not pin the CLI.

The SDK raises the same ValueError deliberately. _normalize_expiration_date wraps date.fromisoformat and re-raises with a readable message (“expiration_date must be a valid date in YYYY-MM-DD format.”) at lines 435-438. The difference is where the error surfaces, not whether it exists: your boundary should reject the date before either the CLI or the SDK has to.

What actually holds at mem0ai 2.2.1

Behaviour Holds at mem0ai==2.2.1? Basis
Expired row suppresses a fresh inferred add() of identical text Yes unfiltered existing_results in Phase 1/5, return [] at 1045
Expiry hides rather than deletes Yes _payload_is_expired used only on read paths
SDK clears an expiry via expiration_date=None Yes, at the cost of one embedding call sentinel at 1871-1873; embed at 2085 before write at 2087
CLI can clear an expiry No no flag; falsy value omitted (#7699)
Metadata- or expiry-only update() calls the embedding provider Yes cache miss in _update_memory, embed at 2085 (#7561)
Impossible CLI date raises uncaught ValueError Reported, not re-executed #7713

Version context: mem0ai 2.2.1 was uploaded 2026-09-25, per PyPI metadata. The npm/TypeScript line is a separate release train (ts-v3.3.1) and is not covered by any claim here.

A write pattern that does not wait for a fix

The fix belongs upstream. Your agent still has to store the preference tonight, so the pattern below removes the dependency on both halves of the suppression: it deletes the hidden row by identity, writes the new fact with a clean dedup set, and asserts visibility instead of trusting the return value.

from datetime import date, datetime, timezone

def _valid_date(s: str) -> str:
    d = date.fromisoformat(s)                       # raises on 2099-02-30
    if d < datetime.now(timezone.utc).date():
        raise ValueError("expiration_date is already in the past")
    return d.isoformat()

def rewrite_fact(mem, text: str, user_id: str, expires: str) -> dict:
    expires = _valid_date(expires)
    # 1. remove any copy that is expired (hidden from reads, still in dedup)
    for old in mem.get_all(filters={"user_id": user_id}, show_expired=True)["results"]:
        if old["memory"] == text and old.get("expiration_date") and \
           date.fromisoformat(old["expiration_date"]) < datetime.now(timezone.utc).date():
            mem.delete(old["id"])
    # 2. write with a dedup set that no longer contains the ghost
    res = mem.add(text, user_id=user_id, expiration_date=expires)
    # 3. assert the outcome the API will not assert for you
    visible = [m for m in mem.get_all(filters={"user_id": user_id})["results"]
               if m["memory"] == text]
    if not visible:
        raise RuntimeError(f"mem0 accepted the write but it is not visible: {res}")
    return {"added": res, "visible_ids": [m["id"] for m in visible]}

Three details make this work rather than merely look tidy. show_expired=True is required on the lookup, because the row you must delete is precisely the one the default read hides. get_all() returns a {"results": [...]} envelope in 2.2.1 and rejects top-level user_id, so both the lookup and the verification index ["results"] and pass the user through filters. The delete happens before the add, so the expired hash is absent from the top_k=10 result set that Phase 5 reads. And the final assertion is on get_all(), not on the return value of add(), because an empty results list is a legal return for “everything was deduplicated”.

The assertion generalizes into a test you can keep:

def test_expired_memory_does_not_block_rewrite(mem, user_id):
    mem.add("user prefers aisle seats", user_id=user_id, expiration_date="2026-01-01")
    assert mem.get_all(filters={"user_id": user_id})["results"] == []        # expired = hidden
    assert len(mem.get_all(filters={"user_id": user_id},
                           show_expired=True)["results"]) == 1               # still stored
    rewrite_fact(mem, "user prefers aisle seats", user_id, "2026-12-31")
    assert len([m for m in mem.get_all(filters={"user_id": user_id})["results"]
                if m["memory"] == "user prefers aisle seats"]) == 1

One operational note that follows from the same code: delete-then-add does not make the embedding provider optional, because add() embeds as well — once for the Phase 1 search query and once per extracted memory. What it changes is where the failure lands. The delete runs first, so a failed add() leaves the fact absent rather than merely stale, which is worse if you cannot retry. If the row must survive a failed write, add a differently-worded copy first, confirm it is visible, and only then delete the expired original. And if you write through the CLI, validate the date yourself before it reaches _validate_expires(); the SDK’s ValueError is useful, the CLI’s uncaught one is not.

This pattern instantiates the vendor-agnostic checks in agent memory write-path reliability: a write is not complete until a read confirms it, and dedup must operate on the same visibility scope as the read path. If you have not set up mem0 yet, the mem0 setup guide covers the configuration this pattern assumes; if the question is whether to stay on mem0 at all, compare frameworks in mem0 vs Zep before debugging expiry, and see the agent memory framework landscape for the wider field.

What this article does and does not establish

Verified by reading the tag, not by running an install: the file at v2.2.1 was fetched on 2026-10-28 and hashed f329ca4a17af1fbefb32ac10d4cc7ae7ddbdb7435a87eb74c30915cff98b8b7c, and the phases, guards, sentinel handling and return [] quoted above are from that file. No live add() or update() was executed for this piece, so the end-to-end failures are reconstructed from the pinned control flow and reported by the issue authors against their own installs — including the update() embed at line 2085, which the #7561 reporter observed on an installed 2.2.1 with only the external embedding boundary mocked. The CLI date defect is likewise reported, with the reporter’s own mocked-backend reproduction, and the CLI is not pinned by the wheel version. Every check here is author-side verification against a public tag you can fetch yourself; no fixture set or evidence directory is offered for download.

Out of scope and not claimed: hosted-platform behaviour, non-Qdrant vector stores beyond the reporter’s local setup, async variants as separately tested code paths (they contain the same unfiltered retrieval and dedup blocks), and any statement about recall quality. The one thing worth carrying away is structural: when a system implements expiry as a read-time filter, every write path that reuses unfiltered search results inherits a memory of things the user can no longer see — and a metadata-only update that re-embeds its own text inherits a provider dependency it never needed.

item.title: Agent Walking-Dead State Detection: How to Detect and Patch Stalled AI Agents
item.description: Detect walking-dead AI agents that run forever but never finish. Learn progress-based detection, work-loop heartbeats, and recovery patterns.
item.content:encoded:
A “walking-dead” AI agent is a process that keeps running, consuming tokens and passing every liveness check, while producing no durable progress toward its task. You detect it not by watching whether the process is alive, but by tracking whether its work actually advances. In one documented case, a SWE-bench Verified agent stayed busy until it used 1.06 million tokens—inspecting, reasoning, and calling tools—yet never wrote the patch, and every health check reported it healthy. This guide shows you how to detect walking-dead states, separate liveness from progress, and patch stalled agents before they burn your budget.

What is a walking-dead state in an AI agent?

A walking-dead agent is a process that is technically running but semantically stuck. It differs from a crash: a crash is visible and easy to detect, while a walking-dead state hides behind a green “alive” status. The process exists, the port responds, CPU and memory look normal, and no error is logged—yet the work has stopped moving.

The core reframing from monitoring research is that “alive/dead” is a false binary. Asking “is the agent alive?” is the wrong question because the answer is almost always yes. The right question is “is the agent making progress?” A walking-dead agent answers that with a quiet no, masked by every conventional health signal.

These failures are far from rare. A July 2026 preprint (“When Agents Do Not Stop” by Hou, Wang, Zhao, and Wang) scanned 6,549 public LLM-agent repositories and manually confirmed 68 infinite-agent-loop failures across 47 projects. Production telemetry shows the same shape: in one deployment, 12% of tasks marked “in_progress” were actually orphaned, with agents dead for hours while their state never changed.

The three signals you are confusing: liveness, health, and progress

Monitoring agents reliably fails because people conflate three distinct signals. Treating them as one produces false negatives exactly where walking-dead agents hide.

Signal What it proves What it misses Typical probes
Liveness The process exists Anything about the work process exists, port responds, PID alive
Health The system can operate Whether work is moving heartbeat HTTP 200, memory, CPU, error logs
Progress Work is advancing Nothing—this is the truth lastProgressAt, monotonic step counter, semantic checkpoints

Liveness and health monitoring catch a frozen process, but they catch none of the walking-dead condition. The agent that burned 1.06 million tokens on SWE-bench Verified passed every liveness and health check. A zombie loop is I/O-bound waiting on LLM responses—it does not spike CPU, does not increase memory, and logs no errors, which is precisely why conventional monitors never flag it.

The fix is to add a third, independent signal: progress. You monitor “is the agent advancing toward completion,” not “is the agent breathing.” This is the difference between a heartbeat that proves a process exists and a progress marker that proves it is not insane.

Why heartbeats lie: work-loop heartbeat vs process-level heartbeat

A “heartbeat” only works if it is emitted from the right place. A process-level heartbeat on a background thread returns HTTP 200 even after the main processing loop has stalled, because the timer thread keeps running while the logic thread is frozen. A watchdog watching that heartbeat concludes “still alive” while the agent does nothing useful.

The correct design is a work-loop heartbeat: a beat emitted from inside the main processing loop, only when the loop actually advances. If the loop stalls, the beats stop. The heartbeat then means “moved forward,” not “still alive.”

Decoupling heartbeat from progress—beating on a timer instead of on advance—defeats the entire watchdog. The whole point of the signal is to detect that forward motion has stopped, so it must be tied to forward motion.

Critically, the watchdog that reads this signal must run as a separate process, not inside the agent. An in-process watchdog freezes together with the agent body it is supposed to watch. If the agent’s loop hangs, so does its internal watchdog, and neither ever reports anything. A separate observer process reads the shared progress file and is insulated from the failure it is meant to catch.

Detecting the stall: no-progress timeouts and semantic checkpoints

Wall-clock timeouts are the naive tool, and they fail because they cannot tell “agent crunching a 10-minute inference” from “zombie holding a lease forever.” A fixed timeout either kills legitimate slow work or lets zombie loops run far too long.

The reliable pattern is a semantic checkpoint in addition to the heartbeat. Track two signals:

  • lastUpdatedAt: the last heartbeat, which proves the agent is alive.
  • lastProgressAt: the last semantic checkpoint, recorded only when the agent reaches a durable milestone (500 rows processed, each file edited, each mutation committed). This proves the agent is not insane.

The rule is simple: heartbeat lost OR progress stalled beyond a timeout means the agent is marked stalled and its task is released back to the pool. One design distinguishes “crunching hard” from “dead”: a heartbeat proves alive, a checkpoint proves sane, and the two together let you tell them apart.

Monitoring research goes a step further and separates activity state from health state. A “waiting” agent that is unhealthy (its context is degraded, its loop is spinning) is a different situation from a “processing” agent that is unhealthy. The first needs a cancel and restart; the second needs an alert, not an interrupt.

Stall thresholds should be per-job-type. Store a stall_sec in job metadata, derived from the longest legitimate step and tuned to a p95 baseline. A 10-second stall might be normal for one task type and catastrophic for another.

The hidden signal: tokens-per-completion and zombie-loop economics

Walking-dead agents are invisible to CPU, memory, and log monitors, but they have one unmistakable signature: token cost per completed unit of work climbs 10–100x. A zombie loop—a repair loop cycling on identical malformed LLM output—shows no CPU spike and no memory growth, but it reliably burns tokens without producing output.

This is why tokens-per-task-completion is a high-signal health metric. Input tokens account for 53.9% of agentic spend, and a single doomed fat-tail session that costs 10x the median can dwarf a whole week of healthy ones. In a 50-task SWE-bench Verified report, 51.4% of the $28.54 total model spend sat on the unresolved, non-converging side. A 30-attempt pilot showed the same shape: 38.9% of spend ($5.24 of $13.48) ended with no result file at all.

The runaway cases are dramatic. One reported subagent recursion consumed 1.2M+ tokens in about 30 minutes with the agent tree still growing; another burned roughly 4M tokens in under 5 minutes, and a 50+ level recursion depth was observed (Claude Code #68619 family).

Token-per-completion turns this invisible waste into a monitorable signal. When cost per completed unit spikes by 10x, you do not need to see the loop—you just see the bill and know something is spinning.

Patching the state: two-stage termination and checkpoint-recoverable work

Once a stall is detected, the recovery action matters as much as the detection. A blanket restart throws away warm context and can make things worse, so pair detection with a deliberate recovery policy.

Two-stage termination is the safe kill sequence. Send SIGTERM first so the agent gets a window to clean up and record an “aborted” note. Only if it fails to exit within the window do you escalate to SIGKILL. This preserves any partial work the agent wrote and leaves a durable trace of how the run ended instead of a silent disappearance.

Checkpoint-recoverable work is what makes restarts cheap. Externalize state at semantic milestones so any stalled task can resume from its last checkpoint instead of cold-starting. In production data, tasks recovered via checkpoint resume complete 3.2x faster than cold starts, and they avoid recomputing idempotent work. This enables exactly-once semantics for non-idempotent operations and lets you release a stalled task back to the pool “with checkpoint intact.”

Loop detection also needs a mechanism. State hashing is a proven approach: hash the prompt plus tool call plus output each step, and if the same hash appears 3+ times within a window, it is looping. An exact-repeat detector works at the action level too: if the same tool call returns the same failure repeatedly, tell the agent to change approach, and let a successful observation clear the streak. Exempt healthy read-only polling so you do not flag legitimate waits.

A recovery decision matrix (activity x health -> action)

A recovery decision matrix maps each (activity x health) combination to the correct action, replacing a one-size-fits-all restart.

Activity state Health state Recommended action
Waiting Healthy Keep waiting; nothing wrong
Waiting Unhealthy Cancel the call, restart fresh
Processing Healthy Continue normally
Processing Degraded Alert, do not interrupt
Looping / non-converging Any Break the loop with a directive, then verify
Stalled (no progress) Any Two-stage kill, then resume from checkpoint

The two key cases to internalize: a “Waiting + Unhealthy” agent should be cancelled and restarted (it is unlikely to recover on its own), while a “Processing + Degraded” agent should be allowed to finish with an alert rather than being interrupted mid-valuable-work. A guardian that is a pure observer—reading the state store but never producing state itself—prevents the monitor from becoming another source of state corruption.

One warning from the research: context saturation maps to “Degraded,” which means a soft warning, not a restart. Filling a context window is not the same as looping; restarting a context-saturated agent can actually lose a lot of useful state and the LLM’s attention. Treat saturation as a warning to let the agent wrap up, not a signal to kill it.

A minimal reference implementation (watchdog + progress marker)

Here is a minimal pattern you can adopt immediately. The agent writes a progress file with two fields, and a separate watchdog process reads it.

# agent.py -- inside the work loop, on each advance
import json, time, os
PROGRESS = "/var/run/agent-state/progress.json"
def mark_progress(step, note):
    with open(PROGRESS, "w") as f:
        json.dump({"step": step, "lastUpdatedAt": time.time(),
                   "lastProgressAt": time.time(), "note": note}, f)

# Call mark_progress() ONLY when work actually advances:
# mark_progress(rows_done, f"processed {rows_done} rows")
# mark_progress(edit_count, f"edited {edit_count} files")

# watchdog.py -- separate process, reads the shared file
import json, time
PROGRESS, STALL_SEC = "/var/run/agent-state/progress.json", 300
while True:
    time.sleep(15)
    try:
        with open(PROGRESS) as f:
            s = json.load(f)
        idle = time.time() - s["lastProgressAt"]
        if idle > STALL_SEC:
            print(f"STALLED: no progress for {idle:.0f}s at step {s['step']}; killing")
            # SIGTERM, wait, then SIGKILL
    except FileNotFoundError:
        print("STALLED: progress file missing; agent never advanced")

The key point is that lastProgressAt only updates on real advance, and the watchdog runs outside the agent. A heartbeat alone is not enough—a timer-driven heartbeat can fire while the work loop is frozen. The progress marker, updated only at semantic milestones, is the signal that proves the agent is not spinning.

Preventing stalls at the source: topology, explicit transitions, idempotency

Detection is necessary, but prevention beats it. Several design choices reduce walking-dead states at their source, before a watchdog ever has to fire.

DAG-shaped agent topologies. Explicit completed/failed transitions between stages prevent the open-ended loops that arise when an agent can wander between states indefinitely. A well-defined task graph leaves fewer ways to get lost.

Hard budgets. A token or time budget caps the worst case. Budgets cannot tell busy work from progress, but they stop a runaway session before it bankrupts a month of token spend. Place a budget checkpoint early—around 60% of the token budget, while tools still work—to write the best partial artifact and ask a blunt convergence question.

Idempotency keys. Enforce exactly-once semantics for every mutation. When a stalled task is released and retried, an idempotency key guarantees the retry does not double-apply side effects. This is what makes checkpoint-resume safe.

Exact-repeat detection baked in. Hashing each step and flagging repeated hashes, or detecting repeated identical tool failures, stops the most common loop shapes cold.

Let the stop decision live outside the model. A model caught in a reasoning loop may never decide to stop on its own. The stop decision belongs to the watchdog and the budget monitor, not to the agent being monitored.

Finally, when you have to stop, save partial work before removing tools. A final no-tools handoff round should produce a human-readable stop reason, not a terse “Agent failed.” This turns a failure into an actionable trace.

FAQ

What is a walking-dead AI agent? A walking-dead agent is a process that keeps running and passing liveness checks while producing no durable progress toward its task. Unlike a crash, it is invisible to conventional health monitoring because CPU, memory, and logs all look normal.

How do I detect a stalled AI agent that is still running? Stop relying on liveness or process-level heartbeats. Add a progress signal: a monotonic step counter and a lastProgressAt timestamp written only when work actually advances, read by a separate watchdog process. Mark the task stalled when progress stalls beyond its job-specific timeout.

Why does a heartbeating agent still get stuck? Because a timer-driven heartbeat continues while the work loop is frozen. Use a work-loop heartbeat that fires only on forward advance, and run the watchdog as a separate process so it does not freeze with the agent body it is supposed to watch.

What is tokens-per-completion, and why does it matter? It is model spend divided by units of work completed. Walking-dead agents spike this 10–100x because zombie loops burn tokens without producing output, while staying invisible to CPU, memory, and log monitors. It is the hidden, reliable health signal for loops.

How do I patch a walking-dead agent without losing work? Use two-stage termination (SIGTERM to let it clean up and record an abort note, SIGKILL only after a window) and externalize state at semantic checkpoints so a stalled task resumes from its last checkpoint instead of cold-starting. Checkpoint resume completes tasks about 3.2x faster than cold starts and enables exactly-once recovery.
